title: Plague, Labour And Late Medieval Europe
text:
I want to trace a chain that runs from a disease to a wage. In the middle of the fourteenth century an epidemic swept across Europe from the east, killing something in the order of a third of the population within a few years and returning in waves for generations afterwards. Its immediate consequences were demographic and religious, but the durable ones were economic.

Before the epidemic, Europe was densely populated relative to the land under cultivation. Land was scarce, labour was abundant, and the terms of that relationship favoured landholders. Afterwards the ratio inverted. Fields stood idle for want of hands, and surviving workers discovered that they could bargain, moving to a better tenancy or demanding higher pay. Authorities in several kingdoms responded with legislation capping wages and restricting movement. Those laws were widely evaded, which itself tells us how far the balance of power had shifted. Over the following century, labour dues eased across much of western Europe and rents fell relative to wages. The lesson is not that plague was beneficial. It is that population size is never merely a number: it sets the relative scarcity of land and labour, and therefore decides who can make demands of whom.
points: A fourteenth-century epidemic killed roughly a third of Europe's population and recurred for generations.
Before it, land was scarce and labour abundant, which favoured landholders.
After it, the ratio reversed: fields lay idle and surviving workers could bargain for better terms.
Governments passed laws capping wages and restricting movement, and these were widely evaded.
Over the next century labour obligations eased and rents fell relative to wages.
The point is that population size sets the relative scarcity of land and labour, and so decides bargaining power.
